# 1. Introduction

Malaria and anaemia remain major causes of morbidity and mortality among
children under five years of age in sub-Saharan Africa, and Tanzania is
no exception. Children in this age group are particularly vulnerable to
malaria because of their developing immune systems and, once infected,
are at increased risk of anaemia. Plasmodium falciparum contributes to
anaemia through the destruction of parasitised and non-parasitised red
blood cells and suppression of bone marrow erythropoiesis (Adam *et
al*., 2025; Mwaiswelo *et al*., 2021; White *et al.,* 2018).

Over the past two decades, Tanzania has invested substantially in
malaria control through the National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP),
including the distribution of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), indoor
residual spraying, seasonal malaria chemoprevention and improved case
management. These efforts have contributed to a decline in national
malaria prevalence, although the burden remains geographically
heterogeneous, with some regions, including Tabora, Kagera and Mtwara,
reporting prevalence several times higher than the national average
(Adam *et al*., 2025; Animut *et al*., 2025).

Anaemia, however, is considerably more common among under-five children
than malaria and has a broader aetiological basis. Contributing factors
include iron and micronutrient deficiencies, poor complementary feeding
practices, intestinal helminths, other infections and household
socioeconomic disadvantage (Elmardi *et al*., 2020; Saidi & Issae,
2025). Consequently, a substantial proportion of childhood anaemia in
Tanzania is likely to occur independently of current malaria infection,
and effective anaemia-reduction strategies cannot rely on malaria
control alone.

This project uses the 2022 Tanzania Demographic and Health Survey and
Malaria Indicator Survey (TDHS-MIS) to examine, among children aged
6--59 months, (i) the prevalence of malaria, anaemia and their
co-occurrence (the "double burden"); (ii) individual-, household- and
community-level factors associated with malaria-related anaemia; (iii)
factors associated with anaemia in the absence of current malaria
infection; and (iv) the extent to which the determinants of these two
forms of anaemia overlap. This progress report summarises the work
completed to date, including the conceptual framing of the problem, a
review of the relevant peer-reviewed literature, the planned analytical
approach and preliminary descriptive findings.

# 2. Problem definition

Preliminary analysis of the 2022 TDHS-MIS data among children aged 6--59
months with complete malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and haemoglobin
results (n = 4,166) illustrates the scale of the problem. Malaria RDT
positivity was 6.1% (255/4,166), whereas anaemia prevalence was 60.5%
(2,521/4,166), approximately ten times higher. The two conditions
co-occurred in 5.1% of children (211/4,166). Thus, among anaemic
children in the sample, 91.6% tested negative for malaria at the time of
the survey, indicating that their anaemia was not accompanied by
detectable concurrent malaria parasitaemia.

This pattern presents an important programmatic and analytical
challenge. National and regional malaria risk-stratification studies in
Tanzania (Adam *et al*., 2025; Animut *et al*., 2025) have mapped
malaria hotspots and their determinants in detail, providing an
appropriate basis for targeting vector-control and case-management
interventions. However, because anaemia is substantially more prevalent
than malaria and is driven by a broader range of factors, interventions
based solely on malaria risk maps may leave a large proportion of the
anaemia burden unaddressed. Conversely, generic anaemia programmes that
do not account for the subgroup of children with malaria-related anaemia
may under-prioritise ITN distribution, prompt diagnosis and treatment,
and seasonal chemoprevention in populations and settings where these
interventions could have the greatest effect on anaemia.

There is therefore a need to move beyond establishing an association
between malaria and anaemia, which is already well documented (e.g.,
Elmardi *et al*., 2020; Mwaiswelo *et al*., 2021; Gena *et al*., 2025;
Saidi & Issae, 2025), towards explicitly separating the anaemia burden
into malaria-related and non-malaria-related components, characterising
the determinants of each and comparing their profiles. This approach
will clarify which risk factors, such as poverty, rural residence, poor
housing and low ITN coverage, are shared across the two pathways and may
therefore benefit from integrated programming, and which are specific to
one pathway, such as dietary and complementary feeding practices for
non-malaria-related anaemia or vector exposure and net use for
malaria-related anaemia and may require targeted interventions.

## 2.1 Research questions

1.  What is the spatial prevalence of malaria infection, anaemia and the
    combined malaria--anaemia double burden (possible malaria related
    anaemia) among children aged 6--59 months in Tanzania, and how does
    this vary across regions/zones and background characteristics?

2.  Which individual-, household- and community-level factors are
    associated with malaria-related anaemia, defined as anaemia
    occurring in the presence of a positive malaria RDT?

3.  Which factors are associated with non-malaria-related anaemia,
    defined as anaemia occurring in children with a negative malaria
    RDT?

4.  To what extent do the determinants identified in Questions 2 and 3
    overlap, and what does the pattern of overlap and divergence imply
    for the design of integrated versus targeted malaria and
    nutrition/anaemia-control interventions in Tanzania?

# 3. Literature survey

Seven peer-reviewed studies were reviewed to situate this project within
the existing evidence on malaria and anaemia among children under five
in Tanzania and comparable sub-Saharan African settings.

## 3.1 Malaria prevalence and determinants in Tanzania

Adam *et al*. (2025), using the 2022 TDHS-MIS, reported a national
malaria RDT-positivity rate of 8% among children aged 6--59 months, with
marked regional variation. Prevalence reached 23% in Tabora but was
below 1% in several central and Zanzibari regions. In multivariable
analysis, older age (24--59 months), rural residence, lower household
wealth and not sleeping under an insecticide-treated net (ITN) were
independently associated with higher odds of malaria infection. The
authors argued that these findings support geographically and
socioeconomically targeted ITN distribution and health education.

Animut *et al*. (2025) extended this national picture through a spatial
and multilevel analysis of the same 2022 TDHS-MIS data. Malaria among
under-five children was significantly spatially clustered (Global
Moran's I = 0.14), with primary hotspot clusters in the Western and Lake
zones and a secondary cluster in Mtwara. Geographically weighted
regression identified household wealth and access to health care as the
strongest spatial determinants of clustering, while multilevel logistic
regression identified maternal education, child age (48--59 months),
family size, low household wealth and unimproved roofing material as
significant individual- and household-level correlates of malaria
infection. This study is methodologically relevant to the present
project because it demonstrates the value of multilevel modelling for
accounting for the clustered structure of DHS data.

## 3.2 Malaria, anaemia and their co-occurrence

Mwaiswelo *et al*. (2021) conducted a community-based malariometric and
socioeconomic survey in Masasi and Nanyumbu districts in southern
Tanzania before the roll-out of seasonal malaria chemoprevention.
Malaria RDT positivity was 15.9% and anaemia prevalence was 53.9%, with
both conditions significantly more common in Nanyumbu than in Masasi.
Anaemia prevalence was higher among malaria-positive than
malaria-negative children in both districts. Multivariable models showed
that district of residence, RDT positivity, lack of bednet ownership or
use, and poor housing characteristics, including thatched roofs and open
eaves, were independently associated with anaemia, alongside child sex
and age. This study provides a directly relevant Tanzanian precedent for
jointly modelling malaria and anaemia and for considering malaria status
as a determinant of anaemia risk.

Gena *et al*. (2025), studying school-aged children in Hawassa,
Ethiopia, reported lower overall prevalence of malaria (8.5%) and
anaemia (9.4%) but a strong association between the two conditions.
Malaria-infected children had more than 13 times the odds of being
anaemic in multivariable analysis, and approximately 29--36% of anaemic
children, depending on the diagnostic method, were also
malaria-positive. Importantly for the present project, most anaemic
children in that study were not malaria infected. Anaemia-specific
determinants included meal frequency and a history of wasting, whereas
malaria-specific determinants included ITN use and caregiver knowledge
of transmission. These findings support the feasibility of statistically
distinguishing malaria-related and non-malaria-related anaemia risk
factors within a single dataset.

## 3.3 Broader determinants of childhood anaemia

Elmardi *et al*. (2020) analysed a large, nationally representative
household survey of children aged 6 months to under 5 years in Sudan and
reported an overall anaemia prevalence of 49.4%, with younger children
(6--23 months) substantially more affected than older children. In the
full cohort, age, place of residence, maternal anaemia and malaria
infection were significant predictors. However, after stratification by
age group, the significant predictors differed: economic status alone
predicted anaemia among children under 2 years, whereas maternal
anaemia, malaria infection and place of residence predicted anaemia
among children aged 2--5 years. This finding is particularly relevant to
the present project because it demonstrates that malaria is one of
several age-varying pathways to childhood anaemia, reinforcing the need
to distinguish malaria-related from non-malaria-related anaemia rather
than treating anaemia as a homogeneous outcome.

Saidi and Issae (2025), in a six-year retrospective hospital-based study
at Morogoro Regional Referral Hospital, Tanzania, documented a decline
in anaemia prevalence among children under five from 72% in 2015 to 33%
in 2020, which they attributed to improving health-care access and
nutrition interventions. Despite this decline, malaria infection
remained the strongest correlate of anaemia in their multivariable model
(adjusted odds ratio ≈ 19.7), followed by age under two years. Dietary
practices, including tea consumption with sugar and high milk intake,
were also significant. This study illustrates that, even within a single
Tanzanian setting, malaria-related and non-malaria-related, particularly
dietary and nutritional, pathways to anaemia coexist and can be
statistically distinguished.

## 3.4 Regional and cross-country evidence

Sacla Aidé *et al*. (2025) analysed the most recent Demographic and
Health Survey data from eight West African countries (Benin, Burkina
Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Guinea, Liberia, Nigeria and Togo) using
generalised linear geostatistical models. ITN use was associated with
significantly reduced odds of malaria infection in four of the eight
countries, while younger child age (under 2 years) was consistently
associated with lower malaria risk across all eight countries. The
authors attributed this pattern to partial protection from maternally
transferred immunity and more consistent net use and caregiver
supervision among infants. National malaria prevalence ranged from below
10% in Ghana to almost 40% in Benin, underscoring substantial
cross-country and, by extension, cross-regional heterogeneity that is
also apparent within Tanzania. These findings support the use of
spatial/geostatistical approaches and adjustment for child age, wealth
and net use when analysing the Tanzanian data.

## 3.5 Synthesis

Taken together, the reviewed literature establishes three points that
motivate the present project. First, malaria and anaemia are strongly
associated but far from co-extensive: anaemia prevalence typically
exceeds malaria prevalence several-fold, both nationally in Tanzania
(Adam *et al*., 2025) and in the districts and countries examined by
Mwaiswelo *et al*. (2021), Gena *et al*. (2025) and Elmardi *et al*.
(2020). Thus, most anaemia cases are not attributable to concurrent
malaria infection. Second, the determinants of malaria, including age,
wealth, residence, ITN use and housing quality, overlap substantially
with broader determinants of anaemia, including maternal anaemia,
dietary practices, wasting, age, wealth and housing, even where the
underlying mechanisms differ. Third, none of the reviewed studies
explicitly partitions anaemia into malaria-related and
non-malaria-related sub-outcomes and formally compares their determinant
profiles within a single national dataset. This represents the specific
analytical gap addressed by the present project using the 2022 Tanzania
TDHS-MIS.

# 4. Approach

## 4.1 Data source and study population

This project uses secondary data from the 2022 Tanzania Demographic and
Health Survey and Malaria Indicator Survey (TDHS-MIS), a nationally
representative, two-stage stratified household survey. The analytic
sample comprises children aged 6--59 months with valid malaria rapid
diagnostic test (RDT) and haemoglobin results from the Household Member
Recode (PR) file, merged as needed with the Household Recode (HR) and
Individual Recode (IR) files for maternal- and household-level
covariates. After excluding observations with missing values for either
outcome component, the working sample comprises 4,166 children.

## 4.2 Outcome variables and case definitions

Anaemia is defined using the WHO haemoglobin threshold for children aged
6--59 months (haemoglobin \< 11 g/dL), consistent with Elmardi *et al*.
(2020) and the TDHS-MIS protocol. Malaria infection is defined as a
positive malaria RDT result, consistent with Adam *et al*. (2025) and
Animut *et al*. (2025).

A key methodological step is the operational separation of
malaria-related from non-malaria-related anaemia. Because the TDHS-MIS
records both anaemia and malaria RDT status for the same child at the
same visit, each child can be cross-classified into four mutually
exclusive groups:

Group A --- Malaria-related anaemia: RDT-positive and anaemic (Hb \< 11
g/dL). This group represents the "double burden" and is used as the
operational definition of malaria-related anaemia.

Group B --- Non-malaria-related anaemia: RDT-negative and anaemic. This
group represents anaemia occurring in the absence of detectable current
malaria infection and is used as the operational definition of
non-malaria-related anaemia in this study.

Group C --- Malaria infection without anaemia: RDT-positive and not
anaemic.

Group D --- Neither condition (reference group): RDT-negative and not
anaemic.

This case definition is consistent with the approach used by Gena *et
al*. (2025), who similarly cross-tabulated malaria and anaemia status to
describe the proportion of anaemic children who were concurrently
malaria-infected. We acknowledge an important limitation of this
definition, which will be addressed explicitly in the final report. An
RDT captures current or very recent parasitaemia and, for HRP2-based
tests, can remain positive for some time after parasite clearance. Thus,
a child classified into Group B could still have anaemia that is a
longer-term physiological consequence of a previous malaria episode. The
four-group classification should therefore be interpreted as
distinguishing anaemia with current, detectable malaria infection from
anaemia without current, detectable malaria infection, rather than as
definitive evidence of causal attribution. Sensitivity analyses
restricting Group B to children with no reported fever during the two
weeks preceding the survey, where available, will be used to assess the
robustness of this classification, following a similar approach to
Elmardi *et al*. (2020).

## 4.3 Explanatory variables

Guided by the reviewed literature, the following individual-, household-
and community-level variables will be extracted and considered as
candidate predictors in both models:

***Child-level***: age in months (categorised, e.g., 6--11, 12--23,
24--35, 36--47, 48--59), sex, nutritional status (stunting/wasting where
available), recent history of fever.

***Maternal-level**:* education, age, anaemia status.

***Household-level*:** wealth index quintile, family/household size, sex
and age of household head, main floor/wall/roof material, availability
and utilisation of ITNs, access to improved drinking water and
sanitation, access to health insurance/health care.

***Community-level***: place of residence (urban/rural), region/zone,
and, where feasible, an indicator of local malaria transmission
intensity derived from cluster-level RDT positivity.

## 4.4 Analytic strategy

Descriptive analysis: Weighted prevalence of malaria, anaemia and each
of the four outcome groups defined in Section 4.2 will be estimated
overall and by region/zone and background characteristics, applying the
DHS sampling weights, strata and primary sampling unit (cluster) design
variables, following the approach of Adam *et al*. (2025) and Animut *et
al*. (2025).

Distinguishing malaria-related from non-malaria-related anaemia
determinants: Two complementary multivariable logistic regression models
will be estimated, both using Group D (neither malaria nor anaemia) as
the reference category:

***Model 1 (malaria-related anaemia):*** Group A versus Group D, to
identify factors independently associated with anaemia occurring
alongside current malaria infection.

***Model 2 (non-malaria-related anaemia):*** Group B versus Group D, to
identify factors independently associated with anaemia occurring in the
absence of detectable malaria infection.

As a robustness check, a single multinomial logistic regression model
with all four groups modelled simultaneously (Group D as the base
outcome) will also be fitted. This approach uses a consistent set of
covariate coefficients and standard errors across the two anaemia
pathways, facilitating formal comparison of coefficients between Groups
A and B. Given the hierarchical structure of the DHS data, with children
nested within households and households within clusters, multilevel
(mixed-effects) logistic models will be used where sample size permits,
following Animut *et al*. (2025) and Elmardi *et al*. (2020).
Cluster-level random intercepts will be included, with reporting of the
intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC), median odds ratio (MOR) and
proportional change in variance (PCV) to quantify the contribution of
cluster-level heterogeneity to each outcome.

***Assessing overlap between the two determinant sets:*** Once Models 1
and 2, together with the multinomial model, are finalised, statistically
significant predictors (p \< 0.05) from each model will be
systematically compared and classified into: (i) shared risk factors ---
variables significant in both models with the same direction of effect;
(ii) malaria-anaemia-specific factors --- significant only in Model 1;
(iii) non-malaria-anaemia-specific factors --- significant only in Model
2; and (iv) divergent factors --- significant in both models but with
opposite directions of association. Based on the literature reviewed in
Section 3, low household wealth, rural residence, lack of ITN use and
poor housing materials are hypothesised to be shared risk factors,
whereas factors closely related to vector exposure and net use may be
specific to malaria-related anaemia, and maternal anaemia,
dietary/feeding practices and other infections may be specific to
non-malaria-related anaemia (Elmardi *et al*., 2020; Saidi & Issae,
2025). The classification will be summarised in a comparison table and
overlap (Venn-style) diagram and will inform the assessment of whether
integrated programming, such as combined ITN distribution and nutrition
education delivered through the same platform, or parallel
pathway-specific interventions are more appropriate for reducing the
overall anaemia burden in Tanzania.

***Model diagnostics*:** Multicollinearity will be assessed using
variance inflation factors, while model fit will be compared using the
Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and deviance, consistent with Animut
*et al*. (2025).

## 4.5 Software and ethical considerations

Analyses will be conducted in Stata or R, using survey/svy or equivalent
packages to incorporate DHS sampling weights, strata and cluster design,
and multilevel packages (e.g., melogit in Stata or lme4/glmer in R) for
mixed-effects models. The study uses secondary, de-identified, publicly
available DHS data obtained through an approved request to the DHS
Program; no new primary data collection involving human participants is
undertaken, and no additional ethical clearance beyond the DHS Program's
existing approvals is required for this secondary analysis.

# 5. Preliminary results

Preliminary descriptive analysis has been completed for the outcome
variables among children aged 6--59 months with complete malaria RDT and
haemoglobin data (n = 4,166). These are unweighted counts, prior to
application of DHS sampling weights and full covariate cleaning, and
will be updated with weighted estimates and confidence intervals in the
next phase of the analysis.

  AND anaemia)

Applying the four-group case definition described in Section 4.2, the
sample can be decomposed as follows:

                                                       sample**

  A: Malaria-related anaemia (RDT+  210                5.1%
  and anaemic)

  (RDT− and anaemic)

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

*Note: Groups sum to N = 4,147 and are internally consistent with the
totals in the indicator table above. Source: Babalola and Annabel's
analysis of the 2022 TDHS-MIS (KR & PR recodes).*

Two preliminary observations follow directly from this decomposition and
motivate the analytic approach in Section 4. First, among anaemic
children (n = 2,521), only 8.4% (Group A, 211/2,521) were concurrently
malaria-positive, while the remaining 91.6% (Group B, 2,310/2,521) were
malaria-negative. This confirms, consistent with the literature reviewed
in Section 3, that the majority of anaemia in this sample was not
accompanied by detectable concurrent malaria infection and therefore
warrants a separate determinant analysis (Model 2). Second, among
malaria-positive children (n = 255), 82.7% (211/255) were also anaemic,
compared with approximately 59% of malaria-negative children
(2,310/3,911), indicating a strong crude association between malaria and
anaemia at the individual level, consistent with Mwaiswelo *et al*.
(2021) and Gena *et al*. (2025). Full multivariable and multilevel
modelling of Groups A and B against the reference Group D, together with
the corresponding overlap analysis of determinants, is planned as the
next stage of the project (Section 4.4).

## 5.1 Spatial distribution of malaria, anaemia and the double burden

Weighted prevalence of malaria, anaemia and the double burden was mapped
at the region and DHS-zone level, and summarised by cluster, to
characterise subnational heterogeneity, following the geospatial
approach of Adam et al. (2025) and Animut et al. (2025).

## 5.2 Distribution by background characteristics

Malaria, anaemia and double-burden prevalence were further examined by
child-, maternal-, household- and community-level characteristics
(Figures 11-14).

![](media/image11.png){width="6.3in"
height="4.295454943132109in"}

*Figure 11. Child-level characteristics. Anaemia was highest among
infants (78.3%) and declined with age; fever, diarrhoea, stunting and
wasting were each associated with higher prevalence of all three
outcomes.*

![](media/image12.png){width="6.3in"
height="4.295454943132109in"}

*Figure 12. Maternal-level characteristics. Anaemia and double-burden
prevalence were highest among adolescent mothers (78.4% and 12.9%,
respectively) and among children of mothers with no education, falling
with increasing maternal education.*

![](media/image13.png){width="6.3in"
height="4.295454943132109in"}

*Figure 13. Household-level characteristics. Malaria and double-burden
prevalence rose sharply with poverty (14.7% and 12.2% among the poorest
vs 0.5% and 0.4% among the richest) and with unimproved roofing (16.2%
vs 4.3% for malaria).*

![](media/image14.png){width="6.3in"
height="4.295454943132109in"}

*Figure 14. Community-level characteristics. Malaria and the double
burden were concentrated in the western (20.1%, 16.7%) and southern
(15.8%, 15.1%) zones and were markedly higher in rural (8.2%, 6.8%) than
urban (0.6%, 0.4%) clusters, while anaemia varied comparatively little
by residence.*

## 5.3 Next steps

a)  Finalise the covariate dataset by merging the PR, HR and IR recodes
    and apply DHS sampling weights, strata and cluster variables.

b)  Estimate weighted descriptive prevalence of malaria, anaemia and the
    double burden by region/zone and key background characteristics.

c)  Fit Model 1 (malaria-related anaemia) and Model 2
    (non-malaria-related anaemia), together with the multinomial and
    multilevel robustness checks described in Section 4.4.

d)  Conduct the overlap analysis of significant determinants and produce
    the comparison table and diagram.

e)  Draft the final report, including full results, discussion,
    limitations and policy recommendations.
